name: Poland
system_note: The directly elected president holds a strong veto.
snapshot: Nationalist President Karol Nawrocki has vetoed bill after bill from Donald Tusk's government, leaving its reform agenda stuck ahead of the 2027 election.
culture: Poland's Catholicism, anchored by John Paul II, the first Polish pope, and the shrine at Częstochowa, is woven into national identity. Chopin, Marie Curie and the Solidarity movement are national icons. The memory of partition, Nazi occupation and communism shapes politics. Pierogi, the Christmas Eve Wigilia supper and a booming video game industry, from The Witcher, are national pride.
society: Poland has been one of Europe's fastest-growing economies since 1989 and now spends more on defence, as a share of GDP, than any other NATO member. It took in millions of Ukrainian refugees in 2022. Society is divided between a liberal, urban west and a conservative, Catholic east, mirrored in the Tusk versus Law and Justice rivalry.
situation: In 2023, Polish voters ousted the nationalist Law and Justice party, which the EU accused of dismantling judicial independence, and brought in Donald Tusk, a former president of the European Council, to restore the rule of law. Then in 2025 they elected a president from the other camp, Karol Nawrocki, a historian and former amateur boxer who once admitted to taking part in football hooligan brawls. In 2026, the two have fought each other to a standstill.

The Polish president does not run the government but can veto laws, and Tusk's coalition lacks the three-fifths majority to override him. Nawrocki has used that power aggressively, vetoing more legislation in his first months than his Law and Justice-aligned predecessor did in a decade (The World This Wiki/Economist digest). He has blocked measures from EU-backed defence loans to tech and crypto regulation, kept the courts reform the government promised stuck, and called for a new constitution by 2030 (Polskie Radio). He opposes Ukraine joining NATO and is demanding huge war reparations from Germany. Tusk's coalition, meanwhile, has fractured, and polls suggest Law and Justice could return in the 2027 parliamentary election. Poland matters well beyond its borders: it is NATO's front line with Russia and Belarus and the main hub for supplying Ukraine.
power: A parliamentary republic with a strong directly elected president. The prime minister leads the government with a majority in the 460-seat Sejm; the president commands the armed forces, shapes foreign policy and holds a veto that takes three-fifths of the Sejm to overturn.
holders: Prime Minister Donald Tusk (Civic Coalition); President Karol Nawrocki, since August 2025.

update.html: The fight over the courts has become an open confrontation. On 30 October the Constitutional Tribunal announced the suspension of its president, Bogdan Swieczkowski, whom the government accuses of blocking judges elected by the current parliament, and Anna Korwin-Piotrowska took charge. That night President Nawrocki flew back from a trip to Senegal and said he helped Swieczkowski back into the building; he then called talks with parliamentary parties, which Tusk's camp boycotted. Tusk vowed no compromise on the rule of law as PiS supporters protested outside the court, and a European Commission spokesperson said appointing tribunal judges lies within the Sejm's power.

story: Poland was a great power with Lithuania until neighbours partitioned it out of existence in 1795. Reborn in 1918, it was invaded by Germany and the Soviet Union in 1939; six million Polish citizens died in World War Two, half of them Jews. Under communism, the Solidarity union led resistance and won the first semi-free elections in 1989. It joined NATO and the EU and became one of Europe's fastest-growing economies.
